content.rendered:
Abram was ninety-nine, still childless, when God appeared with a new name and a command that only made sense if the name was true: El Shaddai.

The Gospel For Today | Tuesday, August 18, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, ‘I am Almighty God; walk before Me and be blameless.’”
Genesis 17:1 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

By the time God appeared to Abram in Genesis 17, the promise of a son was thirteen years old and still unfulfilled. Abram had already tried to help God along by fathering Ishmael through Hagar, a decision that solved nothing and created new complications. At ninety-nine, with Sarah’s body as dead as his own for the purpose of bearing children, God did not show up with a new strategy. He showed up with a new name: El Shaddai, God Almighty.

Scholars trace Shaddai to a root meaning “sufficient” or “all-sufficient,” and some connect it to the Hebrew word for breast — the image of a God who nourishes and sustains completely, whose supply does not run dry. Whatever the precise etymology, the point of the name in context is unmistakable: this is the God for whom biological impossibility is not an obstacle. He does not need Abram’s schemes. He needs Abram’s walk — before Him, blameless, trusting the name to be true before the evidence caught up.

The New Living Translation renders the moment plainly: “I am El-Shaddai — ‘God Almighty.’ Serve me faithfully and live a blameless life.” (Genesis 17:1 NLT). Notice the order: the name comes first, the instruction second. God does not ask Abram to walk blamelessly and then earn the revelation of who He is. He reveals who He is first — Almighty, all-sufficient — and the blameless walk becomes possible because of what has just been revealed, not before it.

A year later, Isaac was born. The name was proven not by argument but by a baby in Sarah’s arms, decades after her body had stopped even trying. That is what El Shaddai does: not incremental improvement on human effort, but supply where human capacity has run out entirely. Paul would later describe this same God as the one “who gives life to the dead and calls those things which do not exist as though they did” (Romans 4:17), pointing directly back to Abraham’s story as the pattern for every believer’s faith.

If your situation looks as impossible today as Sarah’s womb looked at ninety-nine — a door that has been closed too long, a body that will not cooperate, a promise that seems to have expired — El Shaddai’s sufficiency does not run out where your capacity does. It starts there.

Prayer

Father, You are El Shaddai, God Almighty, all-sufficient. Where my strength and my timeline have run out, You are not limited. I lay down every scheme I have tried to force a promise into being on my own. Teach me to walk before You in faith, trusting Your sufficiency instead of my own effort. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

My God is El Shaddai, the Almighty, the all-sufficient One. What is impossible for me is not impossible for Him. I will not force what only He can bring to pass. I walk before Him in faith, and I trust His timing.
